mcqs.question: A candidate writes a fully correct, efficient solution in near-total silence. Why might this score lower than a candidate who talks through a slightly rougher solution?
options: Silent coding is against most interview platform rules
Correctness is weighted lower than the other three rubric dimensions
The debrief has little evidence beyond "the code worked," so it can't distinguish real reasoning from a memorized answer
Interviewers are instructed to fail any candidate who doesn't narrate
mcqs.explanation: The debrief only captures what left a trace during the round. A silent-but-correct solution and a memorized-but-correct solution look the same on paper, so the write-up can't credit reasoning it never observed. There's no rule against silence and correctness is still weighted heavily — the issue is missing evidence for the other dimensions.

mcqs.question: How does rubric weighting typically shift between a junior candidate and a senior/staff candidate?
options: Correctness is dropped entirely at senior level
Communication and trade-off reasoning carry more weight at senior level, since that mirrors the job itself
Code quality stops mattering once you're senior
The weighting is identical at every level by design
mcqs.explanation: Correctness stays a baseline expectation, but senior and staff rounds lean harder on communication and complexity trade-offs because those skills are core to the job — explaining decisions, not just producing them. Code quality still matters, judged against production habits rather than dropped.

mcqs.question: A candidate spends 20 of their 45 minutes just reaching a stated approach. What does that leave them exposed to?
options: Nothing — approach discussion is the most heavily weighted phase
Almost no time left to code and essentially none to test, which caps how much evidence they can produce
An automatic fail regardless of what happens next
Extra time is always granted to compensate
mcqs.explanation: The round's time budget is fixed and testing is usually the first casualty when approach discussion runs long — leaving code untested is exactly the kind of gap the rubric penalizes. It isn't an automatic fail and extra time isn't a given; pacing awareness is what prevents this squeeze.

mcqs.question: Why is one rough round more recoverable in a large-company multi-round loop than in a startup's single-round format?
options: Large companies never fail candidates who solve the problem
Startups always run harder problems than large companies
A multi-round loop combines several independently scored rounds, so one weak data point is diluted; a single round often carries the whole decision
Startups don't use rubrics at all
mcqs.explanation: Averaging or committee review across several rounds means one stumble competes with multiple other data points. A startup's one or two rounds have no such cushion — a rough round can BE the entire signal. Startups can still use informal rubrics; they just lack the averaging effect.

mcqs.question: What's the most reliable fix for the "solved it correctly but still got rejected" outcome?
options: Solve harder problems in practice until this stops happening
Produce visible evidence for communication, complexity, and code quality during the round, not just a working answer
Ask the interviewer directly why they failed you
Memorize more solutions so recall is faster next time
mcqs.explanation: This failure mode is almost always a missing-evidence problem, not a missing-skill problem — the fix is producing narration, stated complexity, and readable structure the debrief can point to. More practice problems or faster recall don't address a silent round; they can make it worse by encouraging speed over narration.

mcqs.question: What distinguishes a staff-level performance from a strong senior performance on the same coding problem?
options: The staff candidate always reaches the optimal complexity faster
The staff candidate writes noticeably less code
The staff candidate treats the problem as something to question and reframe, and keeps production habits intact under time pressure, rather than just solving it fast
The staff candidate skips clarifying questions to save time
mcqs.explanation: At staff level, raw problem-solving speed is assumed; the differentiator is questioning the problem's framing and preserving real engineering habits — error handling, naming — under the clock. Skipping clarifying questions is generally a mistake at any level, not a staff-level shortcut.
